facts.title: Ancient Olympic Athletes Competed Naked
facts.summary: For most of the history of the ancient Olympic Games, athletes competed in the nude.

facts.title: Ancient Roman Concrete Outlasts Modern Concrete in Seawater
facts.summary: Roman concrete is not simply stronger than modern concrete, but it is far more durable in the sea: Roman harbor structures have lasted about 2,000 years with little wear, while modern concrete exposed to saltwater can deteriorate within…

facts.title: Australia's Coat of Arms Shows Two Animals That Can't Easily Walk Backward
facts.summary: The kangaroo and emu holding up Australia's coat of arms are often said to symbolise progress, because neither animal can easily walk backwards.

facts.title: Basketball Was Invented by a Canadian
facts.summary: Basketball was invented in December 1891 by James Naismith, a Canadian born on November 6, 1861, in Almonte, in what is now Ontario.

facts.title: Antwerp's Boerentoren Was One of Europe's First Skyscrapers
facts.summary: The Boerentoren in Antwerp, Belgium, completed in December 1931, was one of Europe's very first tall buildings.

facts.title: Bermuda Is Called the Shipwreck Capital of the Atlantic, With Over 300 Wrecks
facts.summary: Bermuda is known as the shipwreck capital of the Atlantic: more than 300 sunken ships, dating from the 1600s to 1997, lie in the waters around the island.

facts.title: Bermuda Is Home to the Gombey Dancers, a Unique Masquerade Tradition
facts.summary: Bermuda's Gombey dancers keep alive a masquerade tradition of dance and drumming that is regarded as an icon of the island.

facts.title: Bjelašnica Mountain Hosted the Men's Alpine Skiing at the 1984 Winter Olympics
facts.summary: Bjelašnica, a 2,067-metre mountain in the Dinaric Alps, hosted the men's alpine skiing events of the 1984 Sarajevo Winter Olympics.

facts.title: Brazil Holds the Record for Most FIFA World Cup Wins
facts.summary: Brazil has won the FIFA World Cup five times, in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002, more than any other nation.

facts.title: British Food Rationing Began in 1940 and Did Not Fully End Until 1954
facts.summary: Food rationing in Britain started on 8 January 1940 and outlasted the war by nine years.

facts.title: British Soldiers Tunnelled Through the Rock of Gibraltar to Aim Cannons
facts.summary: During the Great Siege of Gibraltar, British soldiers dug a tunnel through the Rock itself so they could fire cannons from its sheer north face.

facts.title: Bubble Wrap Was Originally Designed as Textured Wallpaper
facts.summary: Bubble wrap began as a failed attempt to make textured wallpaper.

facts.title: Georgi Ivanov Became Bulgaria's First Cosmonaut in 1979
facts.summary: On 10 April 1979, Georgi Ivanov became the first Bulgarian in space, launching from Baikonur aboard Soyuz 33 with Soviet cosmonaut Nikolai Rukavishnikov as part of the Intercosmos programme.

facts.summary: The world's first official UFO landing pad, according to Guinness World Records, was built in 1967 in St.

facts.title: Yonge Street Was Once Listed as the World's Longest Street
facts.summary: Guinness World Records once listed Toronto's Yonge Street as the longest street in the world, at 1,896 km, but the street itself is only about 86 km long.

facts.title: Cleopatra Lived Closer to the Moon Landing Than to the Pyramids
facts.summary: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.

facts.title: Dawson City Briefly Became the Largest Community West of Winnipeg
facts.summary: During the Klondike Gold Rush, Dawson City briefly became the largest community in Canada west of Winnipeg and north of Seattle.

facts.title: Diego Maradona's "Hand of God" Goal Remains Infamous in Football History
facts.summary: On 22 June 1986, Diego Maradona put the ball into England's net with his hand in a World Cup quarter-final, and the referee allowed the goal.

facts.title: Earth Has Gone Through Five Major Mass Extinctions
facts.summary: Scientists recognize five major mass extinctions in Earth's history, known as the Big Five: short spans when species died out far faster than new ones appeared.

facts.title: Chile's 1960 Earthquake, the Strongest Ever Recorded, Shook for About 10 Minutes
facts.summary: The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in southern Chile, the most powerful ever recorded, shook the ground for about 10 minutes.

facts.title: Eritrea's Italian-Built Railway Climbs From the Red Sea to 2,394 Meters
facts.summary: Eritrea's narrow-gauge railway, built under Italian colonial rule, climbs from the Red Sea port of Massawa to a high point of 2,394 meters just east of Asmara.

facts.title: Fireworks Were Invented in China, With the Earliest Dating to the Song Dynasty
facts.summary: Fireworks were invented in China, and the earliest known ones date from the Song dynasty, which ruled from 960 to 1279.

facts.title: Ghana Is Named After a Medieval Empire That Lay Far to Its Northwest
facts.summary: Modern Ghana took its name from the medieval Ghana Empire, which lay far to the northwest, largely in today's southern Mauritania and western Mali.

facts.title: Ghana's Elmina Castle Is the Oldest European Building in Sub-Saharan Africa
facts.summary: Elmina Castle on Ghana's coast, built by the Portuguese in 1482, is the oldest surviving European building in sub-Saharan Africa.

facts.title: Godzilla Was Created as a Metaphor for Nuclear Weapons
facts.summary: Godzilla, who first appeared in Toho's 1954 film Godzilla, was conceived as a metaphor for nuclear weapons.

facts.title: Gold Found at Rabbit Creek on August 16, 1896 Sparked the Klondike Gold Rush
facts.summary: On 16 August 1896, gold was found on Rabbit Creek, soon renamed Bonanza Creek, in Canada's Yukon, setting off the Klondike Gold Rush.

facts.title: Hot Chocolate Began as a Bitter, Spiced Mesoamerican Drink
facts.summary: Long before it became a sweet treat, chocolate was a bitter, frothy drink in Mesoamerica, often flavoured with chilli, vanilla or honey.

facts.title: In France, You Can Legally Marry a Deceased Person
facts.summary: In France, a living person can legally marry a partner who has already died, provided the President of the Republic authorises it.

facts.title: Kendo Is a Modern Japanese Martial Art Based on Samurai Swordsmanship
facts.summary: Kendo, meaning 'the way of the sword', is a modern Japanese martial art descended from kenjutsu, the swordsmanship of the samurai.

facts.title: Kites Were Invented in China Around the 5th Century BC
facts.summary: Kites were invented in China, where the 5th-century BC philosophers Mozi and Lu Ban are credited with flying the first ones.

facts.title: Leningrad's Bread Ration Fell to 125 Grams a Day During the Siege
facts.summary: During the siege of Leningrad, the bread ration for children, the elderly and the unemployed fell to 125 grams a day by November 1941.

facts.title: Marie Curie Is the Only Person to Win Nobel Prizes in Two Different Sciences
facts.summary: Marie Curie is the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

facts.title: Monaco Has Competed at More Olympics Than Any Nation Without a Medal
facts.summary: Monaco has taken part in more Olympic Games than any other nation without ever winning a medal in an Olympic sport.

facts.title: Navajo Code Talkers Sent More Than 800 Error-Free Messages at Iwo Jima
facts.summary: During World War II, about 400 Navajo men served in the US Marine Corps as Code Talkers, passing battlefield messages in a code built on their own language.

facts.title: Neptune Was First Spotted in Aquarius, Where Mathematics Said It Would Be
facts.summary: When Neptune was first identified on September 23, 1846, it lay in the constellation Aquarius, just north of Saturn in the sky.

facts.title: New Zealand Was the First Country to Give Women the Right to Vote, in 1893
facts.summary: On 19 September 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in the world in which all women had the right to vote in parliamentary elections.

facts.title: Quebec City Is North America's Only Walled City North of Mexico
facts.summary: Quebec City's old town is still enclosed by its colonial ramparts, making it the only intact fortified colonial settlement in North America north of Mexico.

facts.title: Roller Coasters Grew Out of 17th-Century Russian Ice Slides
facts.summary: The roller coaster is believed to descend from the "Russian Mountains," hills of ice built in the 17th century in the area that is now Saint Petersburg, which riders slid down on sleds.

facts.title: The Attack on Pearl Harbor Killed 2,403 Americans on December 7, 1941
facts.summary: Just before 8 a.m.

facts.title: The Beaver Became an Official Symbol of Canada in 1975
facts.summary: The beaver became an official symbol of Canada on March 24, 1975, when the National Symbol of Canada Act received royal assent.

facts.title: The Cayman Islands Have About 140 Recorded Shipwreck and Maritime Sites
facts.summary: The Cayman Islands National Museum has recorded 140 maritime sites, shipwrecks among them, across Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman.

facts.title: The Dunkirk Evacuation Rescued 338,226 Troops When Planners Hoped for 45,000
facts.summary: Between 27 May and 4 June 1940, Operation Dynamo evacuated 338,226 Allied soldiers from Dunkirk in northern France as German forces closed in.

facts.title: America's First Alarm Clock Could Only Ring at 4 AM
facts.summary: In 1787, Concord, New Hampshire, clockmaker Levi Hutchins built an alarm clock that could ring at only one time: 4 a.m.

facts.title: The First Item Sold on eBay Was a Broken Laser Pointer
facts.summary: The first item ever sold on eBay, then called AuctionWeb, was a broken laser pointer that went for $14.83.

facts.title: The First Modern Olympic Games Were Held in Athens in 1896
facts.summary: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece, from 6 to 15 April 1896.

facts.title: The Great Fire of London Officially Killed Only Six People
facts.summary: The Great Fire of London destroyed much of the city in September 1666, yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, traditionally six.

facts.title: The Elbow Reef Lighthouse Is Still Hand-Cranked and Burns Kerosene
facts.summary: The Elbow Reef Lighthouse on Elbow Cay, in the Abaco Islands of the Bahamas, is one of only three manually operated lighthouses left in the world.

facts.title: The Kindertransport Carried About 10,000 Children to Safety Without Their Parents
facts.summary: In the months before World War II, about 10,000 children, most of them Jewish, were brought to safety in Britain from Germany, Austria, Czechoslovakia and Poland through the rescue effort known as the Kindertransport.

facts.title: The Name Canada Comes From an Iroquoian Word for Village
facts.summary: The name Canada most likely comes from kanata, a St.

facts.title: The Name United Nations First Appeared in a Wartime Declaration in 1942
facts.summary: The name "United Nations" was born during World War II, before the organization itself existed.

facts.title: The North-West Mounted Police Kept the Klondike Gold Rush Remarkably Orderly
facts.summary: The Klondike Gold Rush stayed unusually law-abiding, largely because of Canada's North-West Mounted Police (NWMP), forerunner of today's RCMP.

facts.title: The RMS Rhone Is a Famous Wreck Dive in the British Virgin Islands
facts.summary: The RMS Rhone, a Royal Mail steamship wrecked off Salt Island in the British Virgin Islands on 29 October 1867, is one of the territory's best-known dive sites.

facts.title: The Shortest War in History Lasted Less Than 45 Minutes
facts.summary: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 lasted roughly 38 to 45 minutes, which is why it is often cited as the shortest war on record.

facts.title: The US Ghost Army Fooled German Forces With Inflatable Tanks and Fake Radio Traffic
facts.summary: One American unit in World War II fought with deception instead of firepower.

facts.title: The White Pass Trail Was So Deadly It Was Called the 'Dead Horse Trail'
facts.summary: During the Klondike Gold Rush, so many pack animals died on the White Pass Trail that it became known as the Dead Horse Trail.

facts.title: The Word 'Sandwich' Is Named After the 4th Earl of Sandwich
facts.summary: The sandwich is named after John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, an 18th-century English aristocrat.

facts.title: The Word 'Trivia' Comes from Latin for 'Three Roads'
facts.summary: The English word trivia comes from Latin trivium, a place where three roads meet, built from tri- (three) and via (road).

facts.title: Tim Berners-Lee Invented the World Wide Web and Gave It Away for Free
facts.summary: British computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN and made the idea freely available, with no patent and no royalties due.

facts.title: Tokyo Once Hosted the World's Largest Fish Market
facts.summary: Until 2018, Tokyo's Tsukiji market was the largest wholesale fish and seafood market in the world.

facts.title: Valentina Tereshkova Became the First Woman in Space in 1963
facts.summary: On 16 June 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova launched aboard Vostok 6 and became the first woman in space.

facts.title: George Washington Had Only One Natural Tooth Left When He Became President
facts.summary: When George Washington was inaugurated as president on 30 April 1789, he had just one natural tooth left, a premolar.
